explain.tweet: The five proofs don’t reach five gods. A purely actual cause can’t have parts, so it can’t be one of a kind, can’t change, can’t be material, can’t be in time, and can’t fail to exist. Deny simplicity and you don’t get a humbler God — you get a creature.
explain.elevator: Once you’ve shown there’s a First Cause that is pure actuality — no unrealized potential at all — a lot follows. Anything with parts has potential, so this cause has no parts. Without parts, there’s nothing that could make two of it, so there’s only one. Change is potential being realized, so it can’t change. Matter is full of parts and potential, so it isn’t material. And existing in time means changing, so it’s timeless. That’s the classical God, and every proof lands on him.
explain.twoMinute:
Here’s the problem this chapter solves. Say you accept an argument that there’s some ultimate cause of the world. Fine — but why call it God? Why one? Why not an impersonal force, or a committee of gods, or a very powerful alien?

Feser’s answer is that the proofs don’t just get you *a* cause; they get you a cause of a very specific sort. It has to be **purely actual** — no potential waiting to be realized — because anything with unrealized potential needs something else to realize it, and then it wouldn’t be first. And from that one feature, the rest follows almost like geometry.

Anything with parts has potential, because the parts have to be combined. So the First Cause has **no parts**: it’s simple. How do you get two of anything? Two dogs differ by their matter; dogs differ from cats by some added feature. Both require parts. So nothing could make there be two First Causes — it’s **one**, necessarily. Change is potential becoming actual, so it **can’t change**. Matter is made of rearrangeable parts, so it’s **immaterial**. Being in time means adding moments and changing state, so it’s **timeless**. And a being whose very essence is to exist can’t fail to exist: it’s **necessary**. Those five descriptions — pure act, simple, existence itself, necessary, the mind behind necessary truths — turn out to be one thing seen from five angles.

Two tools make this work. First, a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have — though it can have it in a higher way, like someone who can print money rather than someone who has cash. Second, our words apply to God **analogically**: “exists” and “knows” are true of God literally, but not in exactly the same way they’re true of us — the way “seeing” a tree and “seeing” a proof are both really seeing.

And the objections? “If God creates, he changes” — no, the change is in the world, the way you can become ‘shorter than your brother’ just because he grew. “A changeless God is dead” — no, life means acting from within, and nothing is more self-active than God. The upshot: if you try to make God more like us — with parts, in time, changing — you don’t get a friendlier God. You get a creature, and the proofs no longer point to it.
explain.eli12:
Imagine the very first domino that starts everything falling — except it isn’t pushed by anything, and it keeps everything going right now, not just at the start. What would it have to be like?

It can’t have any “not yet” in it — nothing it’s waiting to become — because then something else would have to make it become that. Things with pieces always have a “not yet” (the pieces could come apart or be arranged differently). So the first cause has no pieces at all.

Now, how can there ever be two of something? Two cookies from the same batch are made of different bits of dough. Chocolate chip and oatmeal cookies differ by what’s added. Both need pieces. The first cause has no pieces, so there can’t be two of it. There’s just one.

Can it change? Changing means becoming something you weren’t yet — but it has no “not yet.” So no. Is it made of stuff, like atoms? Stuff has pieces, so no. Does it get older? Getting older is changing, so no — it’s outside of time, like an author who thinks up a whole story all at once.

When we say it “knows” or is “powerful,” we mean something real, but bigger than our knowing and power — like how “seeing” a picture and “seeing” a math answer are both really seeing, just different kinds.
whiteboard: Draw five arrows from the left edge labeled Change, Parts, Abstract truths, Essence ≠ existence, PSR, all converging on one circle at the right. Say: five proofs, five starting points — the question today is whether they hit one target and what it’s like.
Inside the circle write PURE ACT = NO POTENCY. Say: this is the master key. Everything else is unpacked from it.

Write the toolbox on the side: (1) PPC — formally / virtually / eminently — with a $20 bill doodle; (2) Action follows being; (3) Univocal / Analogical / Equivocal on a spectrum line, with ‘seeing a tree / seeing a proof’ in the middle.
Draw a line from PURE ACT to NO PARTS (simplicity): parts → potency, so no potency → no parts. Add the reverse arrow to show they entail each other; do the same for EXISTENCE ITSELF and NECESSARY.

Draw two stick figures labeled ‘human 1’ and ‘human 2’ with a bracket: ‘differ by matter’; draw ‘human’ vs ‘dog’ with ‘differ by specific difference.’ Cross both out next to the circle: no parts → no way to be two → ONE.
Draw a thin arrow from God to a small globe labeled ‘world begins.’ Write ‘real change here’ at the globe and ‘Cambridge change’ at God; sketch Socrates and a growing Plato beside it.

Write IMMUTABLE, IMMATERIAL, TIMELESS, NECESSARY as spokes radiating from the circle; for each, write its one-line reason (no potency to actualize / matter = parts + potency / time = succession + stages / contingency = potency + parts).
Draw a book with ‘beginning–middle–end’ and a single lightning bolt from an ‘author’ figure outside the book: God causes all times in one act; ‘at t1’ belongs to the effect, not the act.

Finally, draw a small figure labeled ‘superangel’ with a crown, and write: deny simplicity → God becomes one of a kind + needs a cause → not the First Cause. Close: the attributes stand or fall together.
explain.keyAnalogy: **The author and the story.** An author who conceives a whole novel in one flash stands outside the story’s timeline, isn’t changed when a character is born or dies, is the source of everything in the book without being one of its characters, and has every character’s traits “eminently” in his imagination without himself being a pirate or a princess. Use it to illustrate timeless causation (the author doesn’t write chapter 1 “before” chapter 10 in the relevant sense), Cambridge change (a character’s birth changes the story, not the author), and the difference between the First Cause and the greatest *character* (theistic personalism makes God the hero of the novel instead of its author). Be explicit about the limits: real authors think in time and are composite; the analogy illustrates relations, not God’s inner nature.

persuade.coreInsight:
The click happens when someone sees that **the divine attributes are not a wish list but a single consequence viewed from different sides**. Once a cause is purely actual — with no unrealized potential — it follows by strict reasoning that it has no parts, can’t be one of many, can’t change, can’t be material, can’t be in time, and can’t fail to exist. These aren’t separate claims stacked up by piety; each is what “no potential at all” means in a different department.

It usually fails to click for one of two reasons. First, people keep **picturing God as a very big person inside the universe** — a being among beings — so every attribute sounds like an arbitrary superpower (“how can a person be timeless?”). The fix is to keep returning to what the proofs actually concluded: not a super-being, but the source of being itself. Second, people assume that our words must apply to God **in exactly the same way** or not at all, so “God knows” sounds either anthropomorphic or empty. The analogy of being — which they already use whenever they talk about “seeing” a solution — dissolves this.

audiences.startingPoint: Assumes causes and effects are physical, emergent novelty is everywhere, and theology’s concepts are vague.
audiences.approach: Start with PPC as a principle they already use: conservation laws, “you can’t get information from nothing,” Churchland’s own inference to materialism. Correct the heirloom misreading with the $20 example and the evolution account (genes + mutation + environment). Then show that the attributes are *derived*, with the same rigor as a proof in physics: no potency → no parts → one, unchanging, immaterial. Use the physics point that science also speaks analogically (curved space, wave-particle duality).
audiences.openingQuestion: Do you think a new biological trait can appear with no contribution from genes, mutation, or environment — literally from nothing?
audiences.avoid: Don’t lead with Church councils or Scripture, and don’t overclaim that thermodynamics proves God; Davies’ point supports PPC, not theism directly.

audiences.who: Committed Christian or theist who pictures God as a person like us
audiences.startingPoint: Loves a relational, responsive God; suspects simplicity, immutability, and timelessness are cold Greek imports.
audiences.approach: Affirm that classical theists say God is personal — intellect and will are ascribed to him. Then show the stakes: a God with parts is unique only by accident (Zeus alone on Olympus) and needs a cause (a superangel). Point out that the whole tradition — Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Maimonides, Avicenna, Luther, Calvin, Lateran IV, Vatican I — held simplicity. Frame immutability as fullness, not inertness: God doesn’t change because he lacks nothing.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God were made of parts, what would hold those parts together — and wouldn’t that be more ultimate than God?
audiences.avoid: Don’t make them feel their prayer life is naive; save the details of God’s knowledge, will, and love for Part B rather than implying the classical God is indifferent.

audiences.startingPoint: Trained on Plantinga, possible worlds, and property talk; finds simplicity incoherent.
audiences.approach: Take Plantinga’s argument seriously and isolate its three assumptions (univocity, Platonic properties, an undiscriminating notion of property). Introduce constituent ontology, the essence/property/accident/relation distinctions, and Geach’s Cambridge properties. On necessity, contrast the essence-first modal method with conceivability-first; ask whether numbers can be ‘imagined away.’
audiences.openingQuestion: When Socrates becomes shorter than Plato because Plato grew, has Socrates acquired a new property?
audiences.avoid: Don’t dismiss contemporary metaphysics wholesale or pretend the modal-collapse debate is settled; acknowledge it as live and point to where the resources are.

audiences.startingPoint: Thinks different traditions’ ultimate beings could be many, or that ‘one God’ is just a cultural preference.
audiences.approach: Walk through the argument for unity: how do you get more than one of anything? Show that multiplicity requires parts, and parts require potency, which the First Cause lacks. Then show the convergence: five independent routes, from different starting points, reach one and the same reality. Note that pagan philosophers (Aristotle, Plotinus) reached this conclusion too — it isn’t sectarian.
audiences.openingQuestion: What makes two things two, rather than one thing described twice?
audiences.avoid: Don’t caricature polytheistic traditions; the target is the metaphysics of ‘god as one of a kind,’ not people’s devotion.

audiences.who: Apophatic mystic or ‘God is beyond all words’ believer
audiences.startingPoint: Holds that nothing positive can be said of God; any description is idolatry.
audiences.approach: Agree that negative theology is a real and indispensable part of the truth — immateriality, immutability, timelessness all tell us what God is not. Then show that pure negation can’t even say that God exists or causes, and so would undercut the very reasons for believing in God. Offer analogy as the way to affirm without reducing God to our size.
audiences.openingQuestion: If we can say nothing positive about God, can we say that God exists?
audiences.avoid: Don’t treat their humility as confusion; present analogy as honoring transcendence, not taming it.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Suppose I grant your five arguments each prove some ‘first cause.’ Why think it’s one thing, let alone God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because of what kind of cause they prove. Take the first: it has to be purely actual — no unrealized potential — or it would need something else to actualize it. Now ask: how do you ever get two of anything?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Two electrons are two because they’re in different places, I suppose.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Right — there’s something about each that differs: location, matter, some added feature. Two things of a kind differ by some part or aspect beyond the kind. But that means composition, and composition means potential — the parts could be otherwise combined. A purely actual cause has none of that. There’s nothing that could make a second one.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Maybe the first cause is purely actual in its existence but has potential in its activity. It could have options about what to do.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Two problems. What something does reflects what it is — a being whose existence is pure act has no source for merely potential activity. And if it had an actual part and a potential part, it would be composite, and composites need something to unite their parts. Then it wouldn’t be first.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Composites need a cause only if they began. Maybe it’s always been composite.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Even a thing that has always existed needs an account of why its parts are combined at all. That’s a question of ontological priority, not temporal priority — like asking what keeps a structure together right now, not when it was built.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine. But when you say this thing ‘knows’ or is ‘powerful,’ you’re just projecting human traits onto a metaphysical abstraction.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: If I meant ‘knows’ exactly as you know, yes. If I meant something totally unrelated, I’d be saying nothing. But there’s a third, everyday option. When you say you ‘see’ a proof, you don’t mean your eyes, and you’re not speaking nonsense — seeing a proof is to your intellect as seeing a tree is to your eyes. That’s analogy, and it’s literal.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Convenient. You invent a semantics just for God.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It isn’t invented for God. Physics needs it for curved space and wave-particle duality, and it’s forced on us by the distinction between potential and actual being before God even comes up: potentiality is real, but not real in exactly the way actuality is.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Plantinga — a theist — says simplicity makes God identical to a property, so God would be an abstract object. That seems fatal.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Only if properties are Platonic abstract objects, if ‘power’ means the same in God as in us, and if every predicate names a property on a par with every other. Classical theists reject all three. A thing’s nature and attributes are real constituents of it, not items in a Platonic heaven. And no classical theist says God is a property; he’s subsistent existence itself.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: But God has some features necessarily and some contingently — he’s necessarily powerful but only contingently a creator. Those can’t be identical.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Agreed — and simplicity doesn’t say they are. When Plato grows and Socrates becomes shorter than him, something new is true of Socrates without anything changing in him. ‘Being Creator’ is like that: the real change is in the world. Simplicity identifies only God’s real, intrinsic perfections.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Still, to create is to do something, and doing is changing. I change when I type.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Every agent you’ve met changes while acting, just as every professor you’ve met is under nine feet tall. Neither is essential. What’s essential to acting is producing an effect. What’s essential to teaching is causing learning, not lecturing in particular.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then your God is frozen — no life, no activity.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Life, classically, is acting from within rather than being pushed from outside. A stone does things only when thrown. We’re partly self-moving but need food and air. God acts with no input at all. That’s not less life; it’s the fullest life.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And timelessness? If God keeps things in existence now and tomorrow, he’s acting now and tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: ‘God causes X to exist tomorrow’ doesn’t mean ‘tomorrow, God causes X.’ Think of an author conceiving a whole novel in one flash: within the story, chapter 10 comes after chapter 1, but the author didn’t produce them in that order.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Last one. I can imagine a world with nothing in it at all — not even God. So God isn’t necessary.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: You can imagine a blank. But you can’t imagine God any more than you can imagine the number four — only numerals. Erasing ‘2 + 2 = 4’ from a mental chalkboard doesn’t make arithmetic contingent. And the right way to find out what’s necessary is to start from what exists and what its nature is. A being whose essence just is existence can’t fail to exist.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I’m not convinced the proofs work. But I see that if they do, you don’t get a bearded sky-king; you get something much stranger.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s exactly right — and much more defensible. Every attempt to make God more like a big person makes him less like the First Cause, and the arguments stop pointing to him.

socratic: If I don’t have a $20 bill but can print one, do I lack what it takes to give you $20?
Can a boy give someone a black eye without having one himself? What does that tell you about ‘a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have’?
When you say ‘I see the answer,’ are you using ‘see’ in the same sense as ‘I see the tree’? In a totally unrelated sense?
Is a possibility something, or nothing? If something, is it real in the same way that what’s actual is real?
What makes two coins two coins, rather than one coin counted twice?
If a being had parts, what would explain why those parts are combined? Could that explanation lie within the being itself?
If Zeus were the only god left on Olympus, would his nature be any different? Would he be God in the sense the proofs require?
When your younger brother outgrows you, have you changed?
Every professor you’ve met has been under nine feet tall. Could there be a nine-foot professor? What does that suggest about ‘every agent changes when it acts’?
Is a being that needs food and air more alive, or less, than one that needs nothing?
Can you picture the number four — not the numeral, the number? If not, what does picturing ‘nothing’ tell you about whether numbers or God could fail to exist?
If God had existed for an infinite amount of time, would he still be adding new moments to his life? Would that be a change?

traps.trap: Presenting the attributes as a list of superlatives (‘God is the most powerful, the oldest, the biggest…’).
traps.fix: Show each attribute as a consequence of pure actuality and simplicity. Always give the derivation, not just the label; the interlocking is what persuades.

traps.trap: Saying analogical language is ‘just a metaphor’ or ‘symbolic.’
traps.fix: Insist that attribution and proper proportionality are literal. Use ‘seeing’ a proof and ‘life’ in plants and angels as examples of literal but non-identical senses.

traps.trap: Defending simplicity as ‘God has only one property.’
traps.fix: Explain that we have many true concepts of God, grounded in many kinds of effects, all applying to one undivided reality; and that contingent relations like ‘Creator’ are Cambridge properties, not identical with his essence.

traps.trap: Conceding that immutability means God is inert or unresponsive.
traps.fix: Reframe: God doesn’t change because he is fully actual, not because he is inactive. Acting is producing effects; life is self-origination of activity. Save the details of knowledge and will for Part B, but don’t concede ‘static.’

traps.trap: Treating timelessness as ‘God lives for infinitely long.’
traps.fix: Distinguish everlasting duration from strict timelessness, and use the author analogy to explain single-act causation of a temporal world.

traps.trap: Answering ‘necessary being’ objections with an ontological argument.
traps.fix: Make clear that Feser’s necessity is derived from what the proofs established from the world; it isn’t read off the definition of a word. Point out that Findlay and Schrader beg the question against those proofs.

traps.trap: Defending PPC as ‘the effect must be like the cause’ and getting refuted by sponge cakes.
traps.fix: Lead with ‘total cause’ and the formal/virtual/eminent distinction; offer the $20 example before any critic raises a counterexample.

connections.note: The introduction promised that the proofs reach the God of classical theism, not a cosmic designer or ‘god of the gaps.’ This module delivers on that promise by deriving the classical attributes and defining classical theism by its commitment to simplicity.

The master premise here — God is pure actuality — is chapter 1’s conclusion, and PPC was first introduced there. Unity, immutability, immateriality, and eternity are all unpacked from pure act; the Parmenides/Heraclitus discussion returns to chapter 1’s defense of change.

Chapter 2’s thesis that composites need an extrinsic cause (even if everlasting) drives the unity and simplicity arguments; chapter 2 also first introduced analogical predication and the physics analogy. Here the One is shown to be identical with the Unmoved Mover.

The Augustinian proof’s divine intellect is identified with the other proofs’ First Cause via necessity. The necessity section also leans on chapter 3’s case that mathematical and logical truths are not mere conventions.

The real distinction of essence and existence supplies a case of real act/potency distinction for the analogy argument; subsistent existence itself is shown convertible with pure actuality and simplicity, and God becomes the primary analogate of being.

The rationalist proof argued directly for a necessary being; this module shows why necessity entails and is entailed by pure actuality and simplicity, and defends the coherence of necessary existence against Findlay, Russell, and Schrader.

Part B continues the derivation: omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility, conservation and concurrence, and miracles. It relies on this module’s tools — agere sequitur esse (for omnipotence and concurrence), PPC (for intellect and goodness), analogy (for all positive attributes) — and answers the questions about knowledge, freedom, and responsiveness that timelessness and immutability raise.

Chapter 7’s replies to “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”, “Maybe the universe itself is the uncaused cause,” “Even if there is a first cause, why think it is God?”, and “The cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument” all lean on this module: only what has potency, parts, or an essence distinct from existence needs a cause; the universe has all three; the First Cause has the classical attributes; and its necessity is derived from the world, not from a definition.

Dawkins’ claim that a designer would be more complex than what it explains is answered by divine simplicity; the “one god further” jibe (Zeus, Thor, and the rest) is answered by this module’s point that the classical God is not a member of any kind — Zeus alone on Olympus would still be just a god; and the charge that the God of the philosophers isn’t the God of ordinary believers draws on the analogy of being and the personal (intellect-and-will) character of the classical God.
The capstone’s synthesis of the five proofs rests on the convergence argument here: five starting points, one purely actual, simple, necessary, eternal God.
